title: Philippines, ASEAN leaders back faster rollout of power, fuel solutions
summary: ASEAN leaders are accelerating regional fuel-sharing and electricity-grid agreements as Middle East conflict disrupts supplies.

blocks.text: People use their phones in front in the press centre during the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on November 15, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines — Southeast Asian leaders moved to accelerate regional fuel-sharing and electricity-grid agreements as conflict in the Middle East continues to disrupt energy supplies and drive up costs.
ASEAN member states backed the full implementation of the ASEAN Petroleum Security Agreement during meetings Sunday, November 15, Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said.

The agreement was originally established to allow member states to share crude oil and petroleum products during supply disruptions. It was expanded to cover liquefied natural gas at the 43rd ASEAN Ministers on Energy Meeting in October 2025.
Lazaro said the petroleum agreement would complement other regional energy-security initiatives, including the ASEAN Power Grid.
The ASEAN Power Grid seeks to link national electricity systems through cross-border infrastructure by 2040, allowing countries to trade power and draw on supplies elsewhere in the region.
ASEAN members signed an enhanced memorandum of understanding on the initiative Sunday.
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin reaffirmed the Philippines' commitment to expanding regional electricity trade and attracting investment in cross-border infrastructure.

"As ASEAN Chair in 2026, the Philippines looks forward to working with fellow Member States and partners to advance cross-border electricity trade, attract investment and deliver a stronger ASEAN Power Grid for our communities and economies," Garin said.

The Philippines also signed a two-year cooperation agreement with the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, aligning its work with the Philippine Energy Plan and the Asia Zero Emission Community initiative.
Under the partnership, the Department of Energy will draw on the institute's regional research to develop strategies addressing the country's growing electricity needs.

Pressure on Philippine energy. The Philippines remains under a State of National Energy Emergency declared in March, when conflict in the Middle East intensified supply pressure around key shipping routes, including the Strait of Hormuz.
Volatile fuel prices have since added to inflationary pressure at home. Headline inflation reached a three-year high of 7.8% in October, driven in part by higher energy and transport costs.

The Super El Niño could place further strain on electricity supplies. The DOE has warned that the weather pattern, expected to persist into mid-2027, could push the Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao grids into red-alert conditions.
